content: Hepatitis B vaccination is the most effective method to prevent HBV infection and its associated complications. Since the initial recommendations in 1982, the guidelines for hepatitis B vaccination have evolved into a comprehensive strategy aimed at eliminating HBV transmission in the United States. A key component of this strategy is the universal vaccination of infants, which not only prevents early childhood HBV infections but also provides long-term protection for adolescents and adults. The strategy also includes routine screening of all pregnant women for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), postexposure immunoprophylaxis for infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers, vaccination of unvaccinated children and adolescents, and targeted vaccination of high-risk unvaccinated adults. These measures have been implemented with significant success. For example, over 95% of pregnant women are now tested for HBsAg, and effective case management ensures high rates of postexposure immunoprophylaxis among infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers. Hepatitis B vaccine has been successfully integrated into the routine childhood immunization schedule, achieving coverage levels comparable to other vaccines. Between 1990 and 2004, the incidence of acute hepatitis B significantly declined, particularly among children and adolescents, due to widespread vaccination efforts. HBV is a bloodborne and sexually transmitted virus. While acute disease and new infections are most common in adults, chronic infection is more likely to occur in individuals infected as infants or young children. Before routine vaccination programs, 30-40% of chronic HBV infections were attributed to perinatal or early childhood transmission. The success of vaccination programs is partly due to the established infrastructure for vaccine delivery and federal support for perinatal HBV prevention programs. Despite these successes, challenges remain. For instance, some infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers do not receive timely postexposure immunoprophylaxis due to errors in maternal HBsAg testing or reporting. Additionally, birth dose coverage of the hepatitis B vaccine remains suboptimal, with only 46% of infants receiving the vaccine at birth in 2004. This is critical because the birth dose acts as a safety net to prevent perinatal infection and provides early protection against HBV. Adolescents also face barriers to vaccination, including fewer healthcare visits and the initiation of high-risk behaviors. To address these challenges, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) has updated its recommendations to improve vaccination rates among infants, children, and adolescents. These updates emphasize universal infant vaccination starting at birth, which not only prevents perinatal and early childhood infections but also facilitates the implementation of universal vaccination recommendations. HBV is a 42-nm DNA virus that primarily replicates in the liver. Infection can be asymptomatic or symptomatic, with an average incubation period of 90 days. Chronic infection occurs in approximately 90% of infected infants and 30% of children under five years old. Chronic HBV infection is associated with long-term complications, including cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Individuals with chronic infection also serve as reservoirs for continued HBV transmission. There is no specific treatment for acute hepatitis B, but chronic HBV infection requires medical evaluation and regular monitoring. FDA-approved therapeutic agents can achieve sustained suppression of HBV replication and remission of liver disease in some patients. Periodic screening for HCC using alpha-fetoprotein or imaging studies can enhance early detection and improve survival outcomes. HBV is highly infectious, with transmission occurring through exposure to infectious blood or body fluids. HBsAg-positive individuals are considered infectious, with those who are also HBeAg-positive being more infectious due to higher viral loads. HBV is stable in the environment and can remain viable on surfaces for over seven days, even in the absence of visible blood. For infants, the primary sources of HBV infection are perinatal transmission from infected mothers and horizontal transmission from infected household contacts. Breastfeeding by HBsAg-positive mothers does not increase the risk of HBV transmission if the infant receives appropriate immunoprophylaxis. However, children who are not infected at birth remain at risk from long-term contact with infected mothers. Hepatitis B vaccination schedules for infants and children typically consist of three or more intramuscular doses. The vaccine is highly immunogenic, with seroprotection rates exceeding 95% when administered according to recommended schedules. A birth dose of the vaccine is critical for effective postexposure prophylaxis and serves as a safety net for infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers who are not identified due to testing errors. Adolescents also benefit from hepatitis B vaccination, with seroprotection rates exceeding 95% when the vaccine is administered in a three-dose schedule. However, no combination vaccines containing hepatitis B antigen are currently approved for use in adolescents aged 11-17 years. Preterm infants weighing less than 2,000 grams at birth have a reduced response to the hepatitis B vaccine if administered before one month of age. Special vaccination schedules may be required for these infants to ensure adequate protection. In summary, hepatitis B vaccination is a cornerstone of public health efforts to eliminate HBV transmission. Continued efforts to improve vaccination coverage, particularly the administration of the birth dose and vaccination of high-risk groups, are essential to achieving this goal.
